column5: God sees creation as very good
column6: The commentary treats hamd as a judgment reached after something is found worthy; Genesis closes creation with God's own evaluative verdict that all he made is very good.

column5: Lord's commendation versus self-commendation
column6: Paul says the approved person is not the one who commends himself but the one commended by the Lord, a precise New Testament analogue to the commentary's tested praise rather than self-attributed praise.

column5: praise from God rather than people
column6: Paul locates a person's praise in God rather than human beings, directly sharpening the commentary's contrast between praise's rightful source and the human craving to receive it.

column5: tested faith resulting in praise
column6: The tested genuineness of faith is said to result in praise, glory, and honor at revelation, closely matching the commentary's account of praise as an approval following trial.

column5: God awesome in praises and doing wonders
column6: In the Exodus victory song, God's incomparable holiness is described as awesome in praises and as doing wonders, joining praiseworthy action to praise after deliverance.

column5: Judge of all the earth does justice
column6: Abraham's question presumes that the judge of all the earth acts justly, a concentrated Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's praise after an objectively righteous judgment.

column5: worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs
column6: The angel commands glory and worship for the Creator of heaven, earth, sea, and water sources at the hour of judgment, gathering the commentary's exclusive worship, worlds, water, and verdict motifs.

column5: song of Moses praises true and just ways
column6: The heavenly song calls the Lord's works great and marvelous and his ways righteous and true, a direct praise-formula counterpart to hamd as a judgment on divine action.

column5: nations worship after God's judgments are manifest
column6: The verse grounds universal worship and glorification of God's name in the manifestation of his righteous judgments, closely matching the commentary's final judgment-and-praise scenes.

column5: rivers clap and hills sing together
column6: Rivers and hills are imagined as applauding and singing, a distinct Hebrew Bible instance of nonhuman creation voicing the praise that the commentary extends beyond human speech.

column5: God comes to judge the inhabited world
column6: The psalm's cosmic celebration is oriented to God's coming judgment of the world with righteousness and equity, providing the necessary verdict side of its nonhuman praise scene.

column5: heavens, earth, mountains, forest, and trees celebrate redemption
column6: Isaiah commands the whole created landscape to shout because God has redeemed Jacob, an especially concrete counterpart to the commentary's cosmic praise that follows a decisive saving act.

column5: witnesses know the one God
column6: God names Israel his witnesses so that they may know and understand him, and denies any god before or after him; this sharply joins the commentary's sign, recognition, witness, and one-Lord themes.

column5: God reigns forever and ever
column6: The Exodus song ends by declaring YHWH's eternal reign, a close counterpoint to the commentary's enduring Rab set against celestial bodies that appear and vanish.

column5: God alone exalted when human pride is brought low
column6: Isaiah's day of judgment lowers human haughtiness so that YHWH alone is exalted, giving a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's critique of self-praise and divided praise.

column5: God knows and weighs human actions
column6: Hannah's song rejects arrogant speech because YHWH knows and weighs deeds, an evaluative setting that illuminates the commentary's hamd as a verdict after appraisal.

column5: God weighs the spirit behind apparently clean ways
column6: Proverbs contrasts human self-assessment with YHWH's weighing of motives, a focused analogue to the commentary's distinction between an act's appearance and its proper judgment.

column5: clouds, rain, and grass on mountains
column6: The psalm gives God the work of covering heaven with clouds, preparing rain, and making grass grow, closely meeting the commentary's cloud-to-soil-to-plant nurturing scene.

column5: blossoming wilderness reveals divine glory
column6: The desert's flowering is said to reveal YHWH's glory and majesty, a specific biblical bridge from cultivated growth to recognition of the Lord.

column5: earth suspended over nothing
column6: Job pictures God stretching the north over emptiness and hanging the earth on nothing, a concrete cosmological parallel to the commentary's Lord who keeps the worlds from slipping away.

column5: God alone possesses immortality
column6: The passage gives eternal honor and dominion to the one who alone has immortality, a Christian formulation that clarifies the commentary's contrast between transient luminaries and the abiding Lord.

column5: covenant made beyond those immediately present
column6: Moses says the covenant is not made with the assembled hearers alone, providing a specific communal-and-transgenerational comparison for the commentary's primal covenantal witness to the Rab.

column5: heaven and earth summoned as covenant witnesses
column6: Moses calls heaven and earth to witness the life-and-death covenant choice, a distinct scriptural use of the worlds as witnesses alongside the commentary's “we witness” scene.

column5: one Father and one Creator bind a people
column6: Malachi asks whether all have one Father and one Creator before naming covenantal betrayal, combining parental creation and binding relation in a way that advances the commentary's Rab imagery.

column5: a people formed to recount divine praise
column6: Unlike the deliberately subjectless praise sentence the commentary identifies in Fātiḥa, Isaiah explicitly gives a formed people the vocation of recounting God's praise; the contrast clarifies two distinct speech acts.

column5: children cry “Abba, Father”
column6: The Spirit's cry of filial address gives a New Testament expression of the intimate child-to-God relation that the commentary develops through nurture, care, and the name Rab.

column5: the sun moves at its Maker's command
column6: Sirach presents the sun's course as obedience to the great Lord who made it, a Jewish sapiential counterpart to the commentary's sun as a created sign rather than a god.

column5: human praise cannot exhaust the Creator
column6: Sirach asks where strength sufficient to praise God can be found because he exceeds all his works; this interpretive reflection helps preserve the commentary's total hamd beyond any individual speaker's act.

column5: honor belongs to one who honors creatures
column6: Ben Zoma defines the honored person by honoring others and anchors the claim in God's honoring those who honor him, a Jewish ethical interpretation relevant to the commentary's refusal of self-seeking praise.
